value_chain_position: Power management & connectors layer — sells power-delivery modules feeding AI/data-center racks and industrial electrification build-outs
cost_curve_verified: Vicor has no unit cost curve (it is an equipment maker, not a commodity producer), so the equivalent test is gross-margin direction: the deterministic proxy reads gross margin 'expanding' with a three-year gain of about 7.4 percentage points, and that AGREES in direction with the company-reported path of 51.2% for 2024 to 57.3% for 2025 to 58.0% in the June 2026 quarter — but the proxy's most recent level (about 52.6%) is roughly five percentage points stale versus the reported 58.0%, it understates current growth (proxy revenue up 11.7% year over year is measured against a base inflated by a one-off $45 million legal settlement, against reported growth of 20.2% in the March quarter and a 2026 guide implying about 33%), and it entirely misses the fact that product-only gross margin FELL about 200 basis points in the June 2026 quarter — a disagreement that matters more than the level.
gm_trajectory: Consolidated gross margin rose 280 basis points to 58.0% in the June 2026 quarter on revenue up 26.9% sequentially to $143.4 million — but essentially all of the expansion is mix: royalty income of roughly $30 million (including $15 million recognised from the licence signed in May 2026) carries almost no cost, and management confirmed on the 21 July 2026 call that product-only gross margin was down about 200 basis points sequentially on plant under-absorption plus a one-off, non-capitalisable cost of relocating equipment. Pricing power is currently being demonstrated by the patent estate, not by the modules.
bull_thesis: Vicor makes the power-conversion modules that step high-voltage electricity down to the roughly one volt an artificial-intelligence processor actually runs on, and after three years of a half-empty factory the business has genuinely inflected. Three things carry the case. First, the order book: the one-year backlog — orders scheduled to ship within twelve months — reached $379.7 million in June 2026, up 26% in a single quarter and about 145% against the $155.2 million reported a year earlier, with management stating that 'relatively little' of the increase comes from licensing and that the strength is broad across high-performance computing, industrial and automated test equipment, and aerospace and defence. That backlog now covers roughly 80% of trailing twelve-month revenue of $474.0 million. Second, operating leverage is arriving: the Andover plant that was a margin drag for three years is 'approaching capacity utilization' on management's own words, and operating margin has moved from minus 0.4% for 2024 to 18.1% for 2025 to 24.3% in the June 2026 quarter. Management raised 2026 revenue guidance twice in two quarters, from about $570 million to over $600 million, and beat its own June-quarter guide of roughly $126 million by 14%. Third, the patent estate has become a cash business rather than a legal expense: a $45 million settlement in mid-2025, royalty revenue of $57.4 million for 2025 (up 23.2%), and a licence signed in May 2026 worth $60 million over two years. A second trade-case investigation was instituted on 11 February 2026 with a final determination expected in 2027, and the 2026 guidance explicitly assumes no new licences until then — so any new licence is upside by construction. Technically the company appears to hold a real lead: second-generation vertical power delivery at 3 amps per square millimetre of current density heading to 5, in a 1.5-millimetre package, against competing solutions management describes as 'barely above 1 amp per square millimetre'. The balance sheet funds all of this without outside money: $453.6 million of cash against about $8 million of total debt, plus a $14.3 million semiconductor-manufacturing tax refund received on 13 July 2026 with more expected. Capital allocation has been sane — roughly $33 million of buybacks in 2025 when the shares were between about $50 and $90, then essentially none in 2026 after a five-fold rise. The conditions this case depends on: the second-generation vertical power delivery programmes must convert to named production ramps on the schedule the sales chief sketched (engagement through 2026, production 'late third quarter, fourth quarter of next year'); the first plant's expansion must land on time; the second plant, sized at two to three times the first, must be sited and staged without a capital-cost surprise; and the two-year licences must be renewed in 2027 rather than lapse.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Vicor is a bad business — it is that the share price has already been paid for a plan that has not happened yet, and that the order book which justifies it has demonstrably broken before. Start with the price. At $229.56 the enterprise value — market value plus debt less cash — is about $10.5 billion against trailing twelve-month revenue of $474.0 million and trailing cash earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $127.6 million. That is roughly 21 times sales and 78 times cash earnings, on a 10.5% return on invested capital. Monolithic Power Systems, the closest listed comparison, earns nearly twice that return on four times the revenue and trades at about 20 times sales and 64 times cash earnings; Advanced Energy Industries trades at 6.3 times sales, Bel Fuse at 4.5 times. Vicor is the most expensive name in its own competitive set with the second-lowest return on capital. Next, the earnings are not what they look like. Reported net income of $145.3 million over the last twelve months converted to only $51.3 million of free cash flow, because roughly $43.5 million of that income is a tax benefit rather than an operating result — deferred tax assets recognised in December 2025, stock-option exercise effects in the March and June 2026 quarters. Normalise the tax line and trailing earnings are closer to $1.85 a share, putting the stock near 124 times normalised profit. The street compounds the error: consensus 2027 earnings of $5.95 a share sit against a consensus operating profit estimate of only $126.5 million, an internally inconsistent model that implicitly assumes very large tax benefits persist. Now the operating risk, priced with numbers. Commodities are an input cost here, not a revenue driver: copper, magnetics and substrate inflation, plus tariffs that ran about $2 million a quarter in 2025 and forced a 10% surcharge on customer invoices from July 2025, hit a US-manufacturing module maker directly in the gross margin. Product-only gross margin already fell about 200 basis points in the June 2026 quarter. The backlog is cancellable and has been cancelled: in the June 2025 quarter book-to-bill fell below 1 and backlog dropped 9.6% on 'order cancellations from customers in China and widespread order placement hesitancy' — and the booking rate is already decelerating, from above 2.0 in the March 2026 quarter to 'above 1... a little bit lower' in June. Customer concentration is unmeasured and probably severe: management has declined for six consecutive calls to name a single customer, and when asked directly in July 2026 whether the lead computing customer was even a 10%-of-revenue customer, would not say; an analyst's unrebutted channel check put that one private wafer-scale computing customer at 25–30% of next year's business. The highest-margin line is the shortest-duration one: management disclosed that recent licences are 'two-year deals that are, in effect, all-inclusive' which expire around the end of 2027 and must be renegotiated, with the leverage to renew them dependent on a trade case that has not been decided. Put a digestion year into 2027 — modules stalling near $330 million as a lumpy lead customer pauses, one licence lapsing to leave royalties near $80 million, legacy brick modules flat at $190 million, gross margin back to 50% against roughly $190 million of operating expense — and the company earns about $110 million of operating profit and $133 million of cash earnings, at which point the market prices it like Advanced Energy or Bel Fuse rather than like Monolithic Power. What confirms the bear: a quarter with book-to-bill below 1, or a September-quarter product gross margin that fails to recover from the June dip, or the December 2026 quarter missing the implied roughly $186 million needed to reach 'over $600 million' for the year. What also confirms it: another quarter of no named design win, given that the second-generation ramp is guided in soft, undated language.
sop_bull: $290 per share (favorable parts, valued on a 2027 run-rate). Advanced Products modules, excluding royalties, at a $560 million run-rate as the first plant fills and second-generation vertical power delivery converts, valued at 16 times sales — a discount to Monolithic Power's current 19.9 times — equals $8.96 billion. Intellectual-property licensing at $140 million, reflecting renewal of the existing two-year deals plus at least one new licence after the second trade case concludes, at 16 times sales equals $2.24 billion. Legacy brick modules at a $215 million run-rate, growing again on aerospace, defence and test-equipment demand, at 4.0 times sales — roughly Bel Fuse's multiple — equals $0.86 billion. Net cash of about $446 million plus expected further semiconductor tax credits equals $0.50 billion. The second-plant capacity option, sized by management at two to three times the first and sited by late 2027, carries an embedded value of about $1.20 billion. Total equity value $13.76 billion on 47.7 million diluted shares equals $288, rounded to $290. Cross-check: that equates to about 34 times a 2028 cash-earnings figure of roughly $390 million, demanding but not absurd for a business compounding above 30%.
sop_bear: $78 per share (adverse parts, assuming the electrification and data-centre order cycle turns against it). Advanced Products modules fall back to a $330 million run-rate as the lumpy lead computing customer pauses its ramp and hyperscalers digest capacity — the June 2025 precedent, when book-to-bill fell below 1 and backlog dropped 9.6% on cancellations — valued at 4.0 times sales for a decelerating hardware maker, equals $1.32 billion. Licensing falls to $80 million as one of the two-year all-inclusive deals lapses at the end of 2027 without renewal and the second trade case fails to deliver fresh leverage, at 4.0 times sales equals $0.32 billion. Legacy brick modules hold at $190 million but re-rate to 2.5 times sales equals $0.475 billion. Net cash of $446 million less roughly $150 million already committed to the second plant equals $0.31 billion. Total equity value $2.43 billion, or about $51 a share on the harshest reading; allowing that the market would still pay something for the patent estate as a call option, the adverse case is set at $78. Cross-check at $78: enterprise value of $3.26 billion against a stalled-year revenue of about $600 million and cash earnings of about $133 million equals 5.4 times sales and 24.5 times cash earnings — roughly where Bel Fuse trades today, and below Advanced Energy. Input costs make this worse, not better: copper, magnetics and tariff inflation land on the cost line of a US-manufacturing module maker, and product-only gross margin was already compressing about 200 basis points in the June 2026 quarter before any cycle turn.
sop_breakdown: Base case, valued on a 2027 run-rate and 47.7 million diluted shares. (1) Advanced Products modules, excluding royalties: $480 million of revenue — a genuine ramp from roughly $257 million annualised today, but below the street's implied figure because the sales chief guided second-generation production ramps to 'late third quarter, fourth quarter of next year', which lands mostly in 2028 — at 13.5 times sales, contributing $6.48 billion. (2) Intellectual-property licensing: $105 million, being roughly $60 million of existing royalties plus $40 million from the May 2026 licence at its $10 million quarterly step, at 11 times sales rather than a pure-licensor multiple because these are two-year all-inclusive contracts that must be renegotiated in 2027 and carry real contingent legal fees, contributing $1.16 billion. (3) Legacy brick modules: $205 million at 3.5 times sales, contributing $0.72 billion. (4) Net cash and semiconductor tax credits: $446 million at 30 June 2026 plus the $14.3 million refund received 13 July and further credits expected, adding $0.49 billion. (5) Second-plant funding commitment: less $0.30 billion, since management has said a second plant is required and is choosing between sites now. Total equity value $8.55 billion, or about $180 a share. Cross-check: that implies an enterprise value of $8.06 billion, equal to 10.2 times my 2027 revenue estimate of $790 million and 29 times my 2027 cash-earnings estimate of $275 million — or 48 times the street's more conservative 2027 cash-earnings estimate of $166 million, which is exactly where Advanced Energy trades today. The figure is defensible under either margin view, which is why it is the base.
risk_reward: Stated as levels, in US dollars per share. The shares trade at $229.56. The base-case sum-of-the-parts value is $180, so the stock currently sits about $50 above fair value — there is no margin of safety at all, and the first move required for a buyer to make money is a further rise in the estimates, not a re-rating. The favorable case is $290, about $60 above the current price. The adverse case is $78, about $152 below it. There is no structural floor: net cash is only about $9.65 a share and net current assets about $12.80 a share, neither of which supports the price, and there is no tender, deal term or announced distribution. The distribution is therefore adverse: substantially more room below than above, from a starting point already above base fair value.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing dated event is the second US International Trade Commission proceeding. Vicor filed its complaint on 12 January 2026 with supplements on 21, 23 and 26 January; the Commission instituted the investigation on 11 February 2026 (Federal Register notice 17 February 2026) into certain power converters, circuit board assemblies and computing systems, over Vicor's patented non-isolated sine-amplitude-converter topology. Management confirmed on the 21 July 2026 earnings call that a final determination is expected in 2027 and that the 2026 revenue guidance deliberately assumes no new licences are signed before it. That is a firm, scheduled regulatory event on a statutory clock, which is why it is classified as a hard, dated catalyst — although the precise target date is not in my sources, only the February 2026 institution and management's 'in 2027' framing. Two related events have already fired and are spent: the first exclusion order and cease-and-desist orders from the February 2025 final determination, and the $45 million litigation settlement recognised in the June 2025 quarter. A third is soft and non-binding: the May 2026 licence worth $60 million over two years is signed and already recognising revenue ($15 million in the June 2026 quarter, $5 million guided for September, then $10 million a quarter), so its re-rating value is largely spent. Per this lane's rules the status is descriptive only and has not been used to move the verdict either way.
peer_comps_note: Measured against the assigned competitor set on trailing twelve-month figures as of 4 August 2026, Vicor is the most expensive name in its own chain while earning close to the lowest return on capital. Vicor: 21.0 times enterprise value to sales, 77.9 times enterprise value to cash earnings, 10.5% return on invested capital. Monolithic Power Systems, the closest comparison and the one that most justifies a premium multiple: 19.9 times sales, 63.5 times cash earnings, 18.2% return on invested capital, on roughly four times Vicor's revenue base. Advanced Energy Industries: 6.3 times sales, 47.2 times cash earnings, 8.5% return. Bel Fuse: 4.5 times sales, 26.0 times cash earnings, 9.2% return. Delta Electronics and Infineon are not priced here. The implied multiple in my base case — about 10 times my 2027 revenue estimate — still sits well above Advanced Energy and Bel Fuse and is justified only by Vicor's faster growth, its owned semiconductor plant and its royalty stream. The current price requires Vicor to hold a premium to Monolithic Power on both measures indefinitely, which the return-on-capital evidence does not support.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not about the business, which the street reads roughly correctly, but about three specific numbers the street has wrong. First, the street's earnings are built on a tax line, not an operating line. The consensus 2027 estimate is $5.95 a share against a consensus operating profit estimate of only $126.5 million — arithmetic that only works if very large tax benefits keep recurring. They will not: the benefits of the last four quarters came from recognising deferred tax assets in December 2025 and from stock-option exercises in the March and June 2026 quarters, both one-time in character. Roughly $43.5 million of the last twelve months' $145.3 million of reported net income is a tax benefit, which is why $145 million of accounting profit produced only $51.3 million of free cash. Any investor anchoring on the trailing $3.12 of earnings per share, or on a 2027 estimate of $5.95, is anchoring on a number that operations did not generate. Second, the street reads expanding gross margin as pricing power. It is mix. The 280-basis-point rise to 58.0% in the June 2026 quarter came from royalty income of roughly $30 million that costs nothing to produce; product-only gross margin fell about 200 basis points, a fact management conceded only when Craig-Hallum's Richard Shannon extracted it. Third, the street treats royalties as recurring. Management disclosed on 21 July 2026 that recent licences are 'two-year deals that are, in effect, all-inclusive', that they expire around the end of 2027, and that they must be renegotiated — a materially shorter-duration asset than the phrase implies, and one whose renewal leverage depends on a trade case that has not been decided. Where the street is directionally right and we do not dispute it: the backlog is real, the plant really is filling, and the technical lead in current density appears genuine. The disagreement is entirely about what should be paid for it. The consensus price target of $347.50, with a high of $400, requires Vicor to sustain a premium to Monolithic Power Systems on both sales and cash-earnings multiples while earning barely half Monolithic's return on invested capital. Note also how thin the coverage is: three or four analysts carry the 2027 and 2028 estimates, and the most recent target, from Needham on 21 July 2026, was a cut to $320 issued the morning after the strongest quarter in the company's history. That is the first crack in the anchor.
valley_of_death: There is no cash-burn hump and no debt wall — Vicor holds $453.6 million of cash against about $8 million of total debt and collected a $14.3 million semiconductor tax refund on 13 July 2026. The risk over the next three to nine months is entirely to the reported numbers and the multiple. Four specific things sit in the window. First, the September 2026 quarter carries a mechanical revenue headwind that many holders have not internalised: the chief financial officer stated plainly that the May 2026 licence contributes $15 million of revenue in the June quarter but only $5 million in September, a $10 million sequential drag that shipments must more than absorb to deliver the guided 'nearly 10%' sequential growth. The quarter is therefore a harder comparison than it looks, and it reports in late October 2026. Second, the gross-margin optic reverses with it: with royalty revenue stepping down, consolidated gross margin will lean far more heavily on the product line that just compressed about 200 basis points, so a September print showing consolidated margin below 58% is likely even if the underlying business is fine — and it will be read as a failure of the pricing-power story. Third, free cash flow is about to get worse before it gets better. Capital spending has already stepped from roughly $4–6 million a quarter through 2025 to $12.4 million and $11.2 million in the two quarters of 2026, construction in progress stands at $18.2 million with $23.5 million still to be spent on the first plant alone, and a second plant sized at two to three times the first is being sited now. Trailing free cash flow of $51.3 million against a $10.9 billion market value is already a 0.5% yield; a capital-spending step-up compresses it further at exactly the moment the market may start demanding cash rather than accounting earnings. Fourth, the demand risk is not theoretical. In the June 2025 quarter book-to-bill fell below 1 and backlog dropped 9.6% on 'order cancellations from customers in China and widespread order placement hesitancy around tariffs', and the booking rate has already decelerated from above 2.0 in the March 2026 quarter to 'above 1... a little bit lower' in June. One quarter of book-to-bill below 1, against a stock at 21 times sales, is a very large drawdown. Underneath all of it sits the unmeasured concentration risk: management would not confirm in July 2026 whether its lead computing customer was even 10% of revenue, while an analyst's unrebutted channel check put that single private wafer-scale customer at 25–30% of next year's business. If that customer's ramp slips a quarter, the module line stalls and there is no disclosed diversification to point to.
positioning_washout: There is no dividend and no yield-focused shareholder base, so the classic mechanical liquidation does not apply. The forced-selling pressure here comes from three other directions, and the first is already in motion. The stock rose roughly 621% in the twelve months to late June 2026 and reached $382.65, then fell to about $214 by 21 July and trades at $229.56 today — roughly 40% below the high and about 19% below its fifty-day average of $284. That drawdown has already flushed the momentum and trend-following money that bought the parabola; what remains is a holder base with enormous embedded gains and a very low cost basis, which is a slow, price-insensitive source of supply on any rally rather than a violent capitulation. The second is structural and quantifiable: diluted shares went from 45.08 million in June 2025 to 47.71 million in June 2026, up about 5.8%, as options struck between roughly $19 and $68 are exercised against a $229 share price. The company received $26.4 million of option proceeds in the June 2026 quarter alone and $17.8 million in March. Every exercise creates shares that are usually sold, and the buyback that would have absorbed them has stopped — Vicor repurchased about $17.5 million of stock in the June 2025 quarter and $15.4 million in September 2025, then essentially nothing since. Insiders are on the same side of that trade: the chief executive sold across 2 and 6 July 2026 at $302 to $328, a director sold on 23 July at $224.72, and the open-market record shows zero purchases against 86 sales. The third is what will not happen: with founder-chief executive Patrizio Vinciarelli holding about 8.35 million shares, roughly 18% of the company, there is no governance path by which an activist forces a strategic process, a spin-off of the licensing business, or a capital return. Anyone underwriting this on activist or break-up optionality should stop; the sum-of-the-parts discount, if one ever emerges, has no mechanism to be closed by anyone other than management.
forcing_function: Three dated events, in order of proximity. First and nearest: the September 2026 quarterly report, due in late October 2026, is the first clean test of whether product revenue can grow enough to absorb the disclosed $10 million sequential step-down in licence revenue and still deliver the guided 'nearly 10%' sequential increase — and whether product-only gross margin recovers from its roughly 200-basis-point June dip. That single report will settle the pricing-power argument that the consolidated margin line currently obscures. Second: the December 2026 quarter, reported in February 2027, must deliver roughly $186 million of revenue for the year to reach the 'over $600 million' guide, against $256.4 million booked in the first half. That is a very steep implied ramp and it either validates or breaks the capacity-fill story. Third, and the genuine re-rating event: the final determination in the second US International Trade Commission investigation, instituted 11 February 2026 and expected by management in 2027. A second exclusion order is the leverage that converts infringing users into licensees, and management has explicitly stated that no new licences are assumed in guidance until it lands. It also arrives in the same year the existing two-year all-inclusive licences expire and must be renegotiated — so 2027 is simultaneously the year the licensing line could step from roughly $100 million toward the 'couple of hundred million' management has described, and the year it could lapse. That is the fork the whole valuation turns on, and it does not resolve within the next twelve months. One further scheduled item worth watching: the second-plant site decision, which management said on 21 July 2026 would 'probably be making decisions in the next few weeks' — a signed site with disclosed capital cost would remove a real unknown from the model.
moderator_conclusion: Wait for the wash-out. This is a genuinely good business at a price that has already been paid for a plan management has not yet executed, and the honest answer is that both halves of that sentence are true at once. Vicor sells the power-conversion modules that step high-voltage electricity down to the roughly one volt an artificial-intelligence processor runs on, and the operating turn is real: revenue up 26.9% sequentially to $143.4 million in the June 2026 quarter, a one-year order book of $379.7 million that is up about 145% year over year and which management attributes mostly to product rather than licensing, operating margin up from roughly break-even in 2024 to 24.3%, a factory that spent three years as a margin drag now 'approaching capacity utilization', $446 million of net cash with no debt, and a patent-enforcement campaign that has produced actual money rather than press releases. Capital allocation has been sane in the way that matters — they bought stock when it was between $50 and $90 and stopped once it multiplied five-fold. That is the profile of a narrow but widening moat built on an enforced patent estate wrapped around a plant the company owns outright, and there is no structural force threatening its terminal value. The problem is arithmetic. At $229.56 the enterprise value is about $10.5 billion against $474.0 million of trailing revenue and $127.6 million of trailing cash earnings — roughly 21 times sales and 78 times cash earnings, on a 10.5% return on invested capital. Monolithic Power Systems, the nearest comparison, earns nearly twice that return on four times the revenue and trades cheaper on both measures; Advanced Energy trades at 6.3 times sales and Bel Fuse at 4.5. Vicor is the most expensive name in its own chain with close to the lowest return on capital, and the reported earnings that make the multiple look tolerable are inflated: roughly $43.5 million of the last twelve months' $145.3 million of net income is a tax benefit, which is why all that accounting profit converted to only $51.3 million of free cash. Reconciling the favorable and adverse parts gives a base sum-of-the-parts value of $180 a share, with the favorable case at $290 and the adverse case at $78. The stock trades about $50 above base fair value, which means there is no margin of safety and the first move a buyer needs is higher estimates, not a re-rating. Two things would change this. The cleanest is price: at or below roughly $160 — a genuine discount to the $180 base, and about 8 times my 2027 revenue estimate — the risk becomes worth taking, and the stock has been below that level within the last twelve months, so this is not an idle level. The other is evidence: a named hyperscaler or large equipment maker awarding a production ramp for second-generation vertical power delivery, disclosed by the company rather than sourced from an analyst's channel checks, would lift my module assumptions materially and move the base case up. Note what is missing today — six consecutive calls without the company naming a single customer, a refusal in July 2026 to confirm whether its lead customer is even 10% of revenue, an unrebutted analyst suggestion that one private wafer-scale computing customer is 25–30% of next year's business, and a design-win schedule described only as 'late third quarter, fourth quarter of next year'. Add the goalpost move — a $2.5 billion, 70%-gross-margin target with no date attached, replacing a $1 billion target the company has not reached — and the case for patience is straightforward. The nearest test arrives in late October 2026, when the September quarter must absorb a disclosed $10 million step-down in licence revenue and show whether product gross margin recovers from its June dip. That report, not the price, is what a director should be waiting on.
